intro: The Talmud has a history of its own, apart from the arguments on its pages. It was put on trial in Paris in 1240 and burned there around 1242. Censors cut its lines. Printers in Venice and Vilna fixed the page that students still open. War destroyed the world where much of its study lived, and survivors printed it again.

Today the Talmud is read in yeshivas, universities, synagogues, law schools and on phones. Scholars compare manuscripts. Women fill halls to celebrate finishing it. Judges in Israel debate its place in law. This unit asks how a book of argument survived and what each new group of readers looks for in it.

By the end you will be able to trace the Talmud from manuscript to print to screen, explain how censorship shaped the text, and compare how traditional, academic and modern readers approach the same page. You will cite dates and passages and attribute every view to the readers who hold it.
bigQuestion: How did the Talmud survive fire, censorship and destruction, and who reads it today?

timeline.t: The Talmud is put on trial at the Paris disputation
About twenty-four wagonloads of Talmud volumes are burned in Paris
A scribe finishes the Munich codex, the only nearly complete manuscript
Daniel Bomberg prints the first complete Babylonian Talmud in Venice
Copies of the Talmud are burned in Rome
The censored Basel Talmud is printed
The Volozhin yeshiva is founded in Lithuania
The Romm press prints the Vilna Shas
Rabbi Meir Shapiro proposes Daf Yomi in Vienna
The Survivors' Talmud is completed in Germany with U.S. Army help
A free English Talmud translation goes online on Sefaria
Siyum HaShas celebrations in New Jersey and Jerusalem

test.q: What happened at the Paris disputation of 1240?
choices: Rabbis answered charges against the Talmud before Christian judges
The Talmud was printed for the first time
test.why: Rabbi Yechiel and others answered Nicholas Donin's charges before judges in Paris.

test.q: Which city saw the first complete printed Babylonian Talmud?
test.why: Daniel Bomberg printed it in Venice in 1520–23.

test.q: Why do Talmud citations use numbers like 2a and 2b?
choices: They follow the leaf numbering from early printed editions
test.why: Bomberg's leaf numbering, with a and b sides, became the standard.

test.q: What did the Basel censors leave out entirely?
test.why: The 1578–81 Basel edition omitted Avodah Zarah, the tractate on idol worship.

choices: The standard printed edition, made by the Romm press in 1880–86
test.why: The Romm press edition became the standard Talmud page.

test.q: What did Rabbi Meir Shapiro propose in 1923?
choices: Studying the same Talmud leaf each day everywhere
test.why: He proposed Daf Yomi at the Agudath Israel gathering in Vienna.

test.q: Why is the Munich codex valuable?
choices: It is the only nearly complete manuscript and predates most censorship
It contains the Vilna Gaon's notes
test.why: Finished in 1342, it preserves readings later censorship changed.

test.q: A historian and a yeshiva student read the same line. What is most likely true?
choices: They ask different kinds of questions of the same page
test.why: Traditional readers stress law and argument; academic readers stress history and text.

test.q: What did the Survivors' Talmud title page show?
choices: A camp with barbed wire below and the land of Israel above
test.why: The image set a labor camp beneath a scene of the land of Israel.

test.q: In Berakhot 10a, what does Beruriah urge Rabbi Meir to pray for?
choices: That the men turn back from their ways
test.why: She reads Psalm 104:35 as asking for sins, not sinners, to end.

test.q: Which group organized the women's Siyum HaShas in Jerusalem in 2020?
test.why: Hadran, a women's Talmud learning group, organized it.

test.q: Which statement about views on women's Talmud study is accurate?
choices: Movements differ, each citing its reading of the sources, such as Mishnah Sotah 3:4
test.why: Ben Azzai and Rabbi Eliezer disagree in Sotah 3:4, and later readers took both sides.

test.q: What does the Cairo Genizah contain?
choices: Hundreds of thousands of fragments, including early Talmud pieces
test.why: The Ben Ezra synagogue's storeroom preserved letters, contracts and text fragments.

test.q: What does Mishnah Bava Metzia 1:1 rule when two hold a garment and each claims all of it?
choices: Each swears an oath and they divide it
test.why: Each swears his share is not less than half, and they divide it.

choices: S. Y. Agnon — 1966 Nobel Prize in Literature
test.why: Agnon shared the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1966.

write.prompt: How did forces outside the Talmud shape the page readers study today? Cite two or three passages or events from the unit (for example Berakhot 2a, Mishnah Bava Metzia 1:1, the Basel edition) and explain what happened to the text and how its readers responded.
tips: Name each text by tractate and page, and each event by place and date.
Attribute every view to the readers or scholars who hold it.
Compare traditional and academic readings rather than judging them.
Use the unit's terms: daf, censorship, manuscript, variant reading, siyum.
